explanations.explanation: That's the one, friend. God says, “Behold, I am sending an angel before you to protect you along the way…” (Exodus 23:20). Out front, watching over the road. I think that's a mighty good traveling companion.

Prophets were around Israel, so I see why that one tempted you. But God doesn't say prophet here. He says, “Behold, I am sending an angel before you…” (Exodus 23:20). The one out front is an angel, and that's the whole answer.

A judge sounds official, I'll give you that. But this verse never mentions one. God says, “Behold, I am sending an angel before you to protect you along the way…” (Exodus 23:20). His messenger on this road is an angel.

Yes, baker. The angel isn't just tagging along. God says he is there “to bring you to the place I have prepared.” (Exodus 23:20). The place is already prepared, and the angel is the one who leads them there.

Careful, this one is true. God says the angel is sent “to protect you along the way and to bring you to the place I have prepared.” (Exodus 23:20). So the angel guards them on the road and brings them to the place. The place is already prepared before they arrive.

explanations.answer: The angel will not forgive rebellion
explanations.explanation: That's what God says. “Do not defy him, for he will not forgive rebellion, since My Name is in him.” (Exodus 23:21). He gives the reason right there in the verse. This is a messenger to take seriously, friend.

explanations.answer: The angel will turn back to Egypt
explanations.explanation: Egypt is the place they just left, so I understand the guess. But the verse never says the angel turns back anywhere. God's reason is that the angel “will not forgive rebellion, since My Name is in him.” (Exodus 23:21).

explanations.answer: The angel will go to another people
explanations.explanation: That's a reasonable thing to worry about, but God doesn't say it. The warning is about rebellion. The angel “will not forgive rebellion, since My Name is in him.” (Exodus 23:21). Nothing there about going somewhere else.

That's right. God says the angel won't forgive rebellion “since My Name is in him.” (Exodus 23:21). That line is why the angel gets such a serious warning. When this messenger speaks, Israel is to listen.

This one is true, friend. God says, “…do not defy him, for he will not forgive rebellion, since My Name is in him.” (Exodus 23:21). His Name is in the angel. That's the reason Israel is told to pay attention and listen.

explanations.answer: Listen carefully to the angel and obey God fully
explanations.explanation: Yes, sir. God says, “But if you will listen carefully to his voice and do everything I say, I will be an enemy to your enemies and a foe to your foes.” (Exodus 23:22). Listening to the angel and doing everything God says go together. The promise follows that.

explanations.answer: March ahead of the angel into every battle
explanations.explanation: Marching out in front sounds brave. But God puts the angel out front: “My angel will go before you…” (Exodus 23:23). What He asks of Israel in verse 22 is listening carefully and doing everything He says.

explanations.answer: Offer Him a sacrifice before every battle
explanations.explanation: Sacrifices matter in other places, but this verse doesn't ask for one. God says, “…if you will listen carefully to his voice and do everything I say, I will be an enemy to your enemies…” (Exodus 23:22). The ask is listening and obeying.

I can see why it reads that way, but it's false. God says, “You must not bow down to their gods or serve them or follow their practices.” (Exodus 23:24). The practices are on the same list as bowing down. Nothing in the verse says one is fine if you skip the other.
That's the answer. God says, “You must not bow down to their gods or serve them or follow their practices.” (Exodus 23:24). Following their practices is on the list too. It isn't an exception.

explanations.answer: Demolish them and smash their sacred stones
explanations.explanation: That's the one. God says, “Instead, you are to demolish them and smash their sacred stones to pieces.” (Exodus 23:24). He's clear and He doesn't leave anything to guess. Israel isn't told to leave those gods alone.

explanations.answer: Leave them standing and stay away from them
explanations.explanation: Staying away is half-right in spirit, but it's not what God says. He says, “you are to demolish them and smash their sacred stones to pieces.” (Exodus 23:24). The instruction is to take them down, not walk past them.

explanations.answer: Carry them off and keep them as plunder
explanations.explanation: Plunder is a natural thing to think of after a win. But God says to demolish them and smash their sacred stones to pieces (Exodus 23:24). Nothing there about carrying them off or keeping them.

You got it, baker. God says, “So you shall serve the LORD your God, and He will bless your bread and your water. And I will take away sickness from among you.” (Exodus 23:25). The blessing and the promise come right after serving Him.
Poverty is a heavy thing, so I get the guess. But the verse says, “And I will take away sickness from among you.” (Exodus 23:25). Sickness is the word God uses there.
Fear is a good guess, since it's a heavy thing to carry. But the verse names something else. God says, “And I will take away sickness from among you.” (Exodus 23:25).

That's what God says. “I will make all your enemies turn and run.” (Exodus 23:27). He sends His terror ahead and throws every nation into confusion. By the time Israel shows up, the enemies are already heading the other way.
That's what you'd expect enemies to do, I know. But God says the opposite. “I will make all your enemies turn and run.” (Exodus 23:27). They're thrown into confusion, not lined up for a fight.
Begging for peace would at least be calm and organized. But God says, “I will make all your enemies turn and run.” (Exodus 23:27). Running is what He names.

Yep, the hornet. God says, “I will send the hornet before you to drive the Hivites and Canaanites and Hittites out of your way.” (Exodus 23:28). Small creature, big job. I'm not here to argue with it.
Locusts are a good guess, since they're famous for showing up in swarms. But this verse says, “I will send the hornet before you…” (Exodus 23:28). The hornet is the one God names.
A scorpion would get my attention, I won't lie. But God says it's the hornet. “I will send the hornet before you to drive the Hivites and Canaanites and Hittites out of your way.” (Exodus 23:28).

That's right, baker. God says, “Little by little I will drive them out ahead of you, until you become fruitful and possess the land.” (Exodus 23:30). The pace is slow on purpose. Israel grows fruitful while the land becomes theirs.
Holy is a good word, and I can see why you reached for it. But this verse says, “…until you become fruitful and possess the land.” (Exodus 23:30). Fruitful is the word God uses.

Wealthy would be a nice thing to hear, I'll admit. But the verse says, “Little by little I will drive them out ahead of you, until you become fruitful and possess the land.” (Exodus 23:30). The word is fruitful.

Yes, sir. God says, “For I will deliver the inhabitants into your hand, and you will drive them out before you.” (Exodus 23:31). He delivers them into Israel's hand, and Israel drives them out. Both parts are in the same verse.
This one is true, friend. God says, “For I will deliver the inhabitants into your hand, and you will drive them out before you.” (Exodus 23:31). It's a promise right alongside the borders He sets.
I see where that comes from, but it's false. God says, “You shall make no covenant with them or with their gods.” (Exodus 23:32). It covers both the nations and their gods. No exception is given.
That's the answer. God says, “You shall make no covenant with them or with their gods.” (Exodus 23:32). The nations are named and so are their gods.

explanations.answer: They would cause Israel to sin against Him
explanations.explanation: That's the reason God gives. “They must not remain in your land, lest they cause you to sin against Me.” (Exodus 23:33). He adds that serving their gods would surely be a snare. The concern is about sin against Him.

explanations.answer: They would take the best fields for themselves
explanations.explanation: That makes sense as a worry, but God never says it. His reason is, “…lest they cause you to sin against Me.” (Exodus 23:33). Fields aren't mentioned in this verse.

explanations.answer: They would grow and outnumber the Israelites
explanations.explanation: Numbers are a natural thing to worry about, but the verse doesn't say that. God says the nations must not remain “lest they cause you to sin against Me.” (Exodus 23:33). That's the reason He gives.
